title: The Stamp Act Crisis
objective: After this level you can explain why the Stamp Act of 1765 set off the cry "no taxation without representation", and what Parliament argued back.
summary: The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed colonial paper. Colonists said only their own representatives could tax them; Parliament answered with virtual representation.

cards.headline: A tax on paper set thirteen colonies arguing.
cards.body: In 1765 Parliament taxed the colonists’ newspapers, contracts and playing cards. The money was not the real fight. The fight was over who had the right to tax them at all.

cards.headline: A stamp on everything
cards.body: After the French and Indian War, Britain faced heavy costs to defend its American colonies, and it wanted the colonists to help pay. Its answer was the Stamp Act of 1765. Legal papers, newspapers, pamphlets, playing cards and even dice had to carry a stamp showing the tax was paid. Picture paying the government a fee every time you bought a paper or signed a lease.

cards.headline: No taxation without representation
cards.body: Colonists argued that free people could be taxed only with their own consent, given through their own representatives, and no colonist sat in Parliament. The Sons of Liberty, formed in the summer of 1765, went further: they destroyed the stamps wherever they found them.

cards.headline: Parliament’s answer: virtual representation
cards.body: British writers replied that the colonists were represented already. Whole English cities, like Manchester, elected no member of Parliament, yet every member was supposed to speak for the entire nation. If that worked for Manchester, why not Boston? Colonists rejected the idea: a Parliament they had never elected could not consent to taxes for them.

cards.headline: Boycott, repeal and a warning
cards.body: Delegates from nine colonies met in New York in October 1765 as the Stamp Act Congress and petitioned against the tax. Colonists also boycotted British goods, and British merchants, watching their sales fall, pressed Parliament to back down. On March 18, 1766, it repealed the Stamp Act. The same day it passed the Declaratory Act, claiming power to bind the colonies “in all cases whatsoever.” The tax was gone. The argument was not.

cards.headline: The Stamp Act: explained
learned: The 1765 Stamp Act taxed printed paper
Colonists: no taxation without our own representatives
Boycotts won repeal, but the Declaratory Act kept the claim

questions.explanation: Legal papers, newspapers, pamphlets, cards and dice had to carry a tax stamp.

questions.prompt: Match each Stamp Act response with what it did.
questions.explanation: The Sons of Liberty destroyed the stamps, the Stamp Act Congress petitioned against the tax, and the Declaratory Act claimed power over the colonies “in all cases whatsoever.”

questions.prompt: Virtual representation and the Declaratory Act made the same claim about the colonies. What was it?

options.label: Colonists could each elect their own members of Parliament
Parliament could rule colonists who elected none of it
Each colonial assembly could veto British laws
Only the king, not Parliament, could tax colonists

questions.explanation: Both said Parliament spoke and legislated for colonists, “in all cases whatsoever,” even though they elected no members.
